sections.passage: A conversation between a student and a housing officer at a university. The student, Maria, is calling to inquire about accommodation options for the upcoming academic year. She mentions that she previously lived in a shared house off-campus but wants to try university housing this time. The housing officer, David, explains the different types of accommodation available: single rooms in halls of residence, shared flats with other postgraduate students, and family apartments for those with dependents. Maria says she is a postgraduate student studying Environmental Science and prefers a quiet environment for studying. David suggests Elm Hall, which is specifically designated for postgraduate students and has a no-noise policy after 10 PM. The rent is 650 pounds per month, which includes all utility bills and internet access. Maria asks about the distance to the Science Faculty building, and David tells her it's approximately a ten-minute walk, though there is also a shuttle bus service that runs every fifteen minutes during term time. Maria then asks about the application deadline, and David explains that she needs to submit her application form along with a copy of her student ID and proof of enrollment by the end of June. He also mentions that a deposit of one month's rent is required upon acceptance, which is refundable at the end of the tenancy agreement provided there is no damage to the property. Maria thanks David for the information and says she will complete the application form online that evening.

text.en: What type of accommodation did Maria previously live in?
text.zh: Maria 之前住的是哪种类型的住所？

text.en: What is Maria studying?
text.zh: Maria 学的是什么专业？

text.en: Which hall does David recommend for Maria?

title.en: Section 2 - Monologue in an everyday social context

sections.passage: Welcome to the Greenfield Community Centre. My name is Sarah and I'm the Activities Coordinator here. I'd like to tell you about the various programs and facilities we offer to local residents. The community centre was established in 1998 and has been serving the Greenfield neighbourhood for over twenty-five years. We are open seven days a week, from 7 AM until 10 PM on weekdays and from 8 AM until 8 PM on weekends. Our fitness centre on the ground floor includes a fully equipped gym with cardiovascular and weight-training machines, a 25-metre swimming pool, and a studio for yoga and pilates classes. Membership costs 45 pounds per month for adults, with a discounted rate of 30 pounds for students and senior citizens. We also offer family memberships at 100 pounds per month, which covers two adults and up to three children under sixteen. On the first floor, we have our arts and crafts workshop, which runs sessions every Tuesday and Thursday afternoon. These sessions are free for members and 5 pounds per session for non-members. The workshop covers painting, pottery, and textile arts, and all materials are provided. Our children's programme operates during school holidays and includes activities such as drama workshops, science experiments, and outdoor adventure trips. For older residents, we run a social club every Wednesday morning with activities including book discussions, board games, and guest speakers on topics of local interest. The centre also has a small café on the ground floor that serves hot and cold meals, snacks, and beverages. The café is open from 9 AM until 5 PM daily and offers a 10 percent discount to all centre members. We recently introduced a loyalty card system where every tenth purchase is free. For more information about any of our programmes or to register for membership, please visit our reception desk or call us on 01onal 456-7890. You can also visit our website at www.greenfieldcc.org where you can download membership forms and view the full schedule of activities.

sections.passage: A conversation between two university students, James and Emily, and their tutor, Professor Williams, about their joint research project on urban wildlife habitats. James and Emily have been studying the population of red foxes in the city of Bristol over the past six months. Professor Williams asks them to summarize their findings so far. James explains that they conducted surveys in three different areas of the city: the suburban residential area of Bishopston, the industrial zone near Avonmouth, and the parkland areas around Ashton Court. They used camera traps and footprint tracking to estimate population density. Emily reports that they found the highest concentration of foxes in the suburban residential area, with an estimated population density of 12 foxes per square kilometre. This was significantly higher than the industrial zone, which had only 3 foxes per square kilometre, and the parkland areas, which had approximately 7 foxes per square kilometre. Professor Williams asks about the reasons for these differences. Emily suggests that the abundance of food sources in residential areas, particularly discarded human food waste in bins, is a major factor. James adds that foxes in residential areas also have access to shelter in garden sheds, under decking, and in disused buildings. They note that foxes in the industrial zone face challenges such as pollution and limited food sources, while parkland foxes have more natural food but face competition from other predators. Professor Williams then asks about the methodology they used to collect data. James explains that they set up 15 camera traps across the three study areas, with 5 cameras in each location. The cameras were left in place for four weeks at a time, and they conducted three separate survey periods. Emily adds that they also used GPS tracking devices on a sample of 8 foxes to monitor their movement patterns and home range sizes. The GPS data revealed that suburban foxes had much smaller home ranges, averaging 0.8 square kilometres, compared to industrial area foxes with ranges of up to 3.5 square kilometres. Professor Williams commends their work but suggests they should also consider seasonal variations in their analysis, as fox behaviour changes significantly between breeding season in winter and the rest of the year. He recommends they conduct additional surveys during the mating season in January and February to compare with their current data, which was primarily collected in spring and summer. He also suggests they look at the impact of recent urban development projects on fox populations and consider collaborating with the local wildlife trust, which has been conducting similar research in neighbouring areas.

sections.passage: Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture is about the history and development of renewable energy sources, with a particular focus on solar power technology. I'll be discussing how solar energy has evolved from a niche scientific curiosity into one of the fastest-growing energy sources in the world. The story of solar power begins in 1839 when French physicist Edmond Becquerel discovered the photovoltaic effect, which is the process by which sunlight is converted into electricity. However, it wasn't until 1954 that researchers at Bell Laboratories in the United States developed the first practical silicon solar cell, which achieved an efficiency of about 6 percent. This was a breakthrough moment, though the technology remained prohibitively expensive for widespread use. During the 1960s and 1970s, solar cells found their first practical application in the space industry, powering satellites and spacecraft. The energy crisis of the 1970s spurred renewed interest in solar power as an alternative to fossil fuels, and governments around the world began investing in research and development. By the 1990s, solar panel efficiency had improved significantly, reaching around 15 percent for commercial panels, and costs had begun to decline. The real transformation came in the 2000s and 2010s, driven largely by manufacturing innovations and economies of scale, particularly in China. The cost of solar panels fell by approximately 90 percent between 2010 and 2020, making solar energy competitive with, and in many cases cheaper than, traditional fossil fuel sources. Today, the most efficient commercial solar panels can convert around 22 percent of sunlight into electricity, while laboratory prototypes have achieved efficiencies exceeding 47 percent using multi-junction cell technology. There are two main types of solar power systems: photovoltaic panels, which convert sunlight directly into electricity, and concentrated solar power systems, which use mirrors or lenses to focus sunlight onto a receiver that generates heat to drive a turbine. Photovoltaic systems are far more common for residential and commercial use, while concentrated solar power is typically used in large-scale power plants in regions with high direct sunlight, such as the deserts of North Africa and the American Southwest. One of the main challenges facing solar energy is intermittency, meaning that solar panels only generate electricity when the sun is shining. This has led to significant research into energy storage solutions, particularly lithium-ion batteries and emerging technologies such as solid-state batteries and hydrogen fuel cells. Another challenge is the environmental impact of manufacturing solar panels, which requires rare earth minerals and energy-intensive processes. However, studies have shown that the carbon footprint of solar panel production is typically offset within two to three years of operation, and panels have a lifespan of 25 to 30 years. Looking to the future, emerging technologies such as perovskite solar cells, which can be printed onto flexible surfaces, and building-integrated photovoltaics, which incorporate solar cells into windows and building materials, promise to further expand the applications and reduce the costs of solar energy. The International Energy Agency projects that solar power will become the largest source of electricity generation globally by 2050, accounting for approximately 30 percent of total electricity production.

sections.passage: Tea is one of the most widely consumed beverages in the world, second only to water. Its history stretches back nearly five thousand years to ancient China, where legend has it that Emperor Shen Nung discovered tea in 2737 BC when leaves from a wild tea tree blew into his pot of boiling water. While this story is likely apocryphal, archaeological evidence suggests that tea was indeed consumed in China as early as the Han Dynasty (206 BC to 220 AD), initially for its medicinal properties. During the Tang Dynasty (618 to 907 AD), tea drinking became a widespread cultural practice, and the scholar Lu Yu wrote the first known treatise on tea, The Classic of Tea, which detailed the cultivation, processing, and preparation of tea. Tea was introduced to Japan by Buddhist monks in the early ninth century, and the Japanese developed their own elaborate tea ceremony, known as chanoyu, which emphasises harmony, respect, purity, and tranquility. The tea ceremony became a central element of Japanese culture and remains so to this day. Tea reached Europe in the sixteenth century through Portuguese and Dutch traders, who brought it from their trading posts in Asia. It quickly became fashionable among the European aristocracy, particularly in Britain, where it was initially an expensive luxury item affordable only by the wealthy. The British East India Company played a crucial role in popularising tea in Britain, and by the eighteenth century, tea had become the national drink. The British passion for tea had profound global consequences. To address the trade imbalance caused by Britain's massive tea imports from China, the British East India Company began growing tea in India, particularly in the regions of Assam and Darjeeling, and in Sri Lanka, then known as Ceylon. This colonial tea industry transformed the economies and landscapes of these regions and established India as one of the world's largest tea producers. The tea trade also contributed to significant historical events, including the Opium Wars between Britain and China in the nineteenth century and the Boston Tea Party of 1773, which was a catalyst for the American Revolution. Today, tea is grown in more than sixty countries, with China, India, Kenya, Sri Lanka, and Turkey being the largest producers. Global tea production exceeded six million tonnes in 2020, and the industry employs millions of people worldwide. The most common types of tea are black, green, oolong, and white, all of which come from the same plant, Camellia sinensis, but differ in their processing methods. Black tea is fully oxidised, green tea is unoxidised, oolong is partially oxidised, and white tea is made from young buds and minimally processed. In recent years, there has been growing interest in specialty and artisan teas, with consumers increasingly seeking out single-origin teas and unique flavour profiles, much as they do with specialty coffee. The health benefits of tea have also attracted considerable scientific attention, with studies suggesting that regular tea consumption may reduce the risk of heart disease, certain cancers, and neurodegenerative conditions, though more research is needed to confirm these findings.

title.zh: 文章2 - 珊瑚礁生态系统

sections.passage: Coral reefs are among the most biodiverse and valuable ecosystems on Earth, often referred to as the 'rainforests of the sea.' Although they cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, coral reefs support approximately 25 percent of all marine species, making them one of the most complex and productive ecosystems in the natural world. Coral reefs are built by colonies of tiny animals called coral polyps, which secrete calcium carbonate to form the hard skeleton that provides the reef's structure. These polyps have a symbiotic relationship with microscopic algae called zooxanthellae, which live within their tissues. The algae photosynthesise and provide the coral with up to 90 percent of its energy needs, while the coral provides the algae with shelter and the compounds they need for photosynthesis. This relationship is also responsible for the vibrant colours associated with healthy coral reefs. There are three main types of coral reefs: fringing reefs, which grow directly from the shore; barrier reefs, which are separated from the coast by a lagoon; and atolls, which form ring-shaped structures around a central lagoon, typically around submerged volcanic islands. The Great Barrier Reef off the coast of Queensland, Australia, is the world's largest coral reef system, stretching over 2,300 kilometres and comprising more than 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands. Coral reefs provide numerous ecosystem services that are vital to human wellbeing. They protect coastlines from the damaging effects of wave action and tropical storms, provide habitats for organisms that are sources of food and medicine, and support the livelihoods of over 500 million people worldwide through fisheries and tourism. The global economic value of coral reef services has been estimated at approximately 375 billion dollars per year. However, coral reefs around the world are under severe threat from a combination of human activities and environmental changes. Climate change is the most significant threat, as rising ocean temperatures cause coral bleaching, a phenomenon in which corals expel their zooxanthellae under stress, turning white and eventually dying if conditions do not improve. The Great Barrier Reef has experienced several mass bleaching events in recent years, including severe events in 2016, 2017, 2020, and 2022. Ocean acidification, caused by increased absorption of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, is another major threat, as it reduces the availability of calcium carbonate that corals need to build their skeletons. Other threats to coral reefs include pollution from agricultural runoff and sewage, overfishing, destructive fishing practices such as blast fishing and cyanide fishing, and physical damage from coastal development and shipping. Invasive species, such as the crown-of-thorns starfish, which feeds on coral polyps, can also cause significant damage to reef systems. Conservation efforts to protect coral reefs include the establishment of marine protected areas, restrictions on fishing and coastal development, and research into coral restoration techniques such as coral gardening and assisted gene flow, which involves breeding heat-tolerant coral strains. Scientists are also exploring the use of probiotics to enhance coral resilience to environmental stress. While these efforts are encouraging, experts warn that without significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions and other measures to address climate change, the long-term survival of coral reefs remains uncertain.

sections.passage: Human beings make thousands of decisions every day, from trivial choices like what to eat for breakfast to life-altering decisions such as choosing a career or a life partner. Despite the central importance of decision-making in our lives, research in psychology and behavioural economics has repeatedly demonstrated that human decision-making is far from rational. Our choices are systematically influenced by cognitive biases, emotional states, and environmental factors that we are often unaware of. One of the most influential contributions to our understanding of decision-making comes from the work of Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, who developed Prospect Theory in the late 1970s. Their research showed that people tend to weigh losses more heavily than equivalent gains, a phenomenon known as loss aversion. For example, the pain of losing 100 dollars is psychologically more intense than the pleasure of gaining 100 dollars. This asymmetry leads people to make risk-averse choices when facing potential gains and risk-seeking choices when facing potential losses, which has profound implications for financial decision-making, consumer behaviour, and public policy. Another well-documented bias is the anchoring effect, whereby people rely too heavily on the first piece of information they encounter when making decisions. In a classic experiment, participants were asked to estimate the percentage of African countries that are members of the United Nations. Before answering, they spun a rigged wheel that landed on either 10 or 65. Those who saw the number 10 gave significantly lower estimates than those who saw 65, despite the fact that the number on the wheel was completely irrelevant to the question. This demonstrates how arbitrary anchors can influence even factual estimates. The availability heuristic is another cognitive shortcut that affects decision-making. People tend to overestimate the likelihood of events that are easy to recall, typically because they are recent, vivid, or emotionally charged. For instance, after hearing about a plane crash, people may overestimate the risk of flying, even though statistically, air travel is far safer than driving. Media coverage amplifies this effect by disproportionately reporting dramatic but rare events, skewing our perception of risk. Social influences also play a significant role in decision-making. The phenomenon of groupthink, first identified by psychologist Irving Janis, occurs when the desire for group consensus overrides individuals' ability to critically evaluate alternatives. This can lead to poor decisions in organisational settings, as demonstrated by historical examples such as the Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961, where members of President Kennedy's advisory group failed to challenge a flawed plan due to pressure to conform. Similarly, the bandwagon effect describes the tendency for people to adopt behaviours or beliefs because many others have done so, regardless of their own analysis. More recently, researchers have explored the role of emotions in decision-making. The somatic marker hypothesis, proposed by neuroscientist Antonio Damasio, suggests that emotions play a crucial role in guiding decisions by creating physiological responses, or somatic markers, that signal the potential outcomes of different choices. Damasio's research with patients who had damage to the prefrontal cortex showed that without the ability to experience emotions, individuals struggled to make even simple decisions, suggesting that purely rational decision-making is neither possible nor desirable. Understanding these biases and influences has practical applications in many fields. In healthcare, awareness of cognitive biases can help doctors make more accurate diagnoses. In finance, understanding loss aversion can lead to better investment strategies. In public policy, insights from behavioural economics have been used to design 'nudges' that guide people towards better choices without restricting their freedom, such as automatically enrolling employees in pension schemes, which significantly increases participation rates. However, critics argue that the nudge approach is paternalistic and may be used to manipulate people rather than genuinely help them, raising important ethical questions about the boundaries of behavioural influence in democratic societies.

text.zh: 卡尼曼和特沃斯基开发了什么理论？

text.en: What is loss aversion?
text.zh: 什么是损失厌恶？

options.en: The tendency to avoid all risks
Weighing losses more heavily than equivalent gains
options.zh: 对损失的重视程度高于同等收益

options.en: The fear of making any decisions
Preferring smaller guaranteed gains over larger uncertain ones
options.zh: 偏好较小的确定收益而非较大的不确定收益

text.en: In the anchoring experiment, what were participants asked to estimate?
text.zh: 在锚定实验中，参与者被要求估计什么？

options.en: The percentage of African UN member countries
options.zh: 非洲联合国成员国的百分比

options.en: The number of countries in Africa

text.en: What is the availability heuristic?
text.zh: 什么是可得性启发式？

options.en: Making decisions based on available resources
options.zh: 基于可用资源做出决定

options.en: Overestimating likelihood of easily recalled events
options.zh: 高估容易回忆起的事件的可能性

options.en: Choosing the most readily available option
options.zh: 选择最容易获得的选项

options.en: Only considering information that is immediately available
options.zh: 只考虑立即可用的信息

text.en: Why do people overestimate the risk of flying after a plane crash?
text.zh: 为什么人们在飞机失事后会高估飞行风险？

options.en: Because plane crashes are easy to recall due to media coverage
options.zh: 因为媒体报道使飞机失事容易被回忆

options.en: Because they have personal experience of crashes
options.zh: 因为他们有坠机的个人经历
因为政府统计数据不可靠

text.en: Who first identified the phenomenon of groupthink?
text.zh: 谁首先发现了群体思维现象？

text.en: Which historical event is used as an example of groupthink?
text.zh: 哪个历史事件被用作群体思维的例子？

options.en: The fall of the Berlin Wall

text.en: What does the bandwagon effect describe?
text.zh: 从众效应描述的是什么？

options.en: The tendency to avoid popular choices
Adopting behaviours because many others have done so
options.zh: 因为很多人采用了某种行为而跟风

options.en: The desire to be unique in decision-making
options.zh: 在决策中追求独特性的愿望

text.en: What does the somatic marker hypothesis propose?
text.zh: 躯体标记假说提出了什么？

options.en: That decisions should be purely rational
options.zh: 决定应该完全是理性的

options.en: That emotions create physiological signals guiding decisions
options.zh: 情绪产生生理信号来指导决策

options.en: That body language reveals true intentions
options.zh: 肢体语言揭示真实意图
体育锻炼改善决策能力

text.en: What happened to patients with prefrontal cortex damage in Damasio's research?
text.zh: 在达马西奥的研究中，前额叶皮层受损的患者会怎样？

options.en: They made better decisions than healthy people
options.zh: 他们做出的决定比健康人更好

options.en: They struggled to make even simple decisions
options.zh: 他们甚至难以做出简单的决定

options.en: They showed no change in decision-making ability
options.zh: 他们的决策能力没有变化

text.en: What is a 'nudge' in behavioural economics?
text.zh: 行为经济学中的'助推'是什么？

options.en: A legal requirement to make certain choices
options.zh: 做出某些选择的法律要求

options.en: A design that guides people towards better choices without restricting freedom
options.zh: 一种在不限制自由的情况下引导人们做出更好选择的设计

options.en: A financial incentive for good behaviour
options.zh: 对良好行为的经济激励

options.en: A punishment for making poor decisions
options.zh: 对做出糟糕决定的惩罚

text.en: What example of a nudge is given in the passage?
text.zh: 文章中给出了什么助推的例子？

options.en: Automatically enrolling employees in pension schemes
options.zh: 自动将员工纳入养老金计划

text.en: What criticism of the nudge approach is mentioned?
text.zh: 文章提到了对助推方法的什么批评？

options.en: It is too expensive to implement
It is paternalistic and may be used to manipulate people
options.zh: 它是家长式的，可能被用来操纵人们

options.en: It has been proven not to work
It only works in laboratory settings
options.zh: 只在实验室环境中有效

text.en: What does the passage suggest about purely rational decision-making?
text.zh: 文章对纯粹理性的决策提出了什么看法？

options.en: It is the ideal that everyone should strive for
options.zh: 这是每个人都应该追求的理想

options.en: It is neither possible nor desirable
It can be achieved through training
It is only possible for highly educated people
options.zh: 只有受过高等教育的人才能做到

prompt.en:
Some people believe that universities should focus on providing academic knowledge and theoretical understanding, while others argue that universities should prioritise practical skills and vocational training to prepare students for the job market.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
prompt.zh:
一些人认为大学应该专注于提供学术知识和理论理解，而另一些人则认为大学应该优先考虑实践技能培训和职业教育，为学生进入就业市场做好准备。

讨论两种观点并给出你自己的意见。

给出你的理由，并包括你自己的知识或经验中任何相关的例子。至少写250个单词。
